records.abstract: Online job advertisements can reveal changing skill demand only when competency mentions are recoverable as auditable text spans. Chinese lacks a large resource that combines explicit span-boundary rules with coverage of different recruitment genres. We present Chinese-SkillSpan, a corpus of 22,840 sentences from four Chinese recruitment sources. It uses a flat, ESCO-derived inventory of language skills and knowledge, knowledge, skills, and transversal skills and competences (LSKT), with Chinese-specific rules for minimal-complete, non-overlapping spans. Language models propose annotation drafts, but human reviewers retain authority over accepted offsets and types under a shared handbook. Its evaluation reference is undergoing final human adjudication, so the current results are provisional estimates. The baseline study shows why the resource is challenging: exact extraction changes with Chinese boundary conventions, and accuracy varies across recruitment sources. Taken together, Chinese-SkillSpan contributes a multi-source span resource, a Chinese-specific annotation and evaluation protocol, and a reproducible baseline and diagnostic suite that exposes category, source, and boundary effects. records.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in computational neuroscience for prediction, classification, representation learning, parameter estimation, and related analytical tasks. In most applications, however, the scientific question and the target quantities are specified in advance. Different model architectures may be optimized or compared, but they are primarily evaluated by how well they answer the same predefined question rather than by what different scientific descriptions and questions their architectural differences might make possible. We propose a different use of AI: to treat architectural variation itself as an experimental epistemic variable. Different AI architectures embody different inductive biases and therefore make different temporal, relational, topological, geometrical, symbolic, or dynamical structures accessible in the same empirical data. records.title: Ceremonial etiquette and official events
records.abstract: Ceremonial etiquette plays an important role in diplomatic protocol and international relations. It regulates the conduct of diplomats and officials during official events and state ceremonies. Proper observance of ceremonial etiquette helps maintain order, respect, and professionalism in interactions between representatives of different countries. Official events such as state visits, diplomatic receptions, international conferences, and signing ceremonies follow specific traditions and protocol rules. These rules include the order of precedence, formal greetings, respect for national symbols, and appropriate dress code. The purpose of this study is to analyze the significance of ceremonial etiquette and its role in the organization of official diplomatic events. The research also highlights how adherence to ceremonial protocol contributes to strengthening diplomatic relations and preventing misunderstandings in international communication.

records.abstract: Abstract Monarchy is one of the oldest truly global social structures. On the eve of the imperial age, most of the world was governed by monarchs. Often, European imperial powers abolished them, imprisoning, killing, or exiling local rulers; in other cases, the imperial powers incorporated the conquered monarchies into new imperial orders of indirect rule. In fact, every country that retained its independence in the era of high imperialism was ruled by a monarch: Ethiopia, China, Japan, the Ottoman empire, Persia (Iran), and Siam (Thailand). This article offers some observations on the relationship between the world’s monarchs in the age of empire by focusing on encounters between European monarchs and those of the few non-European countries that retained their independence.

In this study, the transformation of Türkiye's security policies in the fight against terrorism will be analyzed. The increase in the activities of terrorist groups worldwide and the emergence of more porous borders have forced governments to transform their security policies and counter-terrorism methods. Türkiye has employed various counter-terrorism methods against the Partiya Karkeren Kurdistane (PKK) since its first attack in Eruh in 1984. In the 1990s, Türkiye used mostly military counter-terrorism methods in its fight against the PKK. However, between 2002 and 2015, Türkiye has prioritized democratic norms and negotiation methods in its attitude towards the PKK. This article analyses the reasons for this transformation.

records.title: Judicial Diplomacy in Refugee Protection Governance: The ECtHR between Crisis Management and Rights-Centred Adjudication
records.abstract: Abstract This article rethinks the European Court of Human Rights’ role in refugee protection by reading its asylum-related case law as acts of judicial diplomacy. Diplomacy here is not institutional outreach; it is the Court’s reasoning practice: how it frames facts, allocates responsibility, and signals the practical limits of discretion under crisis pressure. This article develops a two-axis framework: (i) anticipatory and crisis-responsive diplomacy, capturing how Strasbourg calibrates tone, scope and evidentiary demands in high-stakes cases and (ii) vertical and horizontal diplomacy, tracking how judgments speak “downwards” into domestic asylum systems and “sideways” across overlapping legal regimes. A close reading of leading decisions on non-refoulement, jurisdiction, and vulnerability shows that the Court’s protective and restrictive strands often follow recurring diplomatic logics rather than mere inconsistency. This article concludes with a rights-centred benchmark for judicial diplomacy: legitimacy in refugee protection turns on making non-refoulement and individualised assessment practically reachable through clear jurisdictional reasoning and effective remedies.

records.title: Global Development Governance in Transition
records.abstract: This chapter examines the transformation of international development cooperation within a changing global order shaped by shifting power relations, security concerns, and evolving state strategies. Moving beyond explanations focused on declining aid volumes, it argues that current developments reflect a structural reconfiguration in the purpose, instruments, and governance of development assistance. From a critical political economy perspective, the analysis shows how financialization, securitization, and fragmentation are reshaping development cooperation into a more strategic and selective domain. Development assistance increasingly operates not as a redistributive mechanism, but as an instrument through which states pursue geopolitical, economic, and security objectives. This shift is reflected in the growing use of investment-oriented instruments, the integration of aid into foreign policy, and the proliferation of actors and competing models. The chapter concludes that development assistance provides a lens for understanding broader transformations in global politics.

records.title: Precedence Among Heads of Mission
records.abstract: Abstract This chapter discusses Articles 16, 17, and 18 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. Article 16 states that, in accordance with Article 13, heads of diplomatic missions take precedence in their respective classes in the order of the date and time of taking up their functions. It also states that any alterations made in the credentials of a head of mission that does not involve the changing of class shall not affect precedence. Lastly, the Article states that it is not prejudiced regarding the precedence of the representative of the Holy See. Article 17 on the other hand states that Ministry for Foreign Affairs or other similar body shall be notified of the precedence of the diplomatic staff, while Article 18 expresses that the procedure to be observed between each respective State for the reception of heads of mission shall be uniform in respect of class.

It is concluded that the modern lawyer must act as an architect of integrity systems, capable of harmonizing profit with social welfare.

records.abstract: This paper examines evolving trends in security crisis management within an increasingly interconnected global environment. The study identifies three primary areas of transformation: technological advancements, collaborative governance frameworks, and emerging threat landscapes. The research highlights the integration of artificial intelligence for threat detection, big data analytics for predictive modeling, and social media monitoring for real-time situational awareness. The analysis demonstrates a paradigm shift toward multi-stakeholder engagement, emphasizing public-private partnerships, international cooperation, and community-based resilience building. Contemporary security challenges—including cyber threats, climate-induced displacement, hybrid warfare tactics, and misinformation campaigns—demand adaptive management strategies that address interconnected risks. Key findings reveal the importance of inclusive governance models that engage diverse stakeholders while maintaining democratic values. The research concludes that effective crisis management requires organizations to prioritize adaptability, collaboration, and proactive engagement over traditional reactive approaches to build resilient communities capable of addressing complex, multifaceted security challenges.

records.title: Between science, authority, and responsibility: Exploring institutional logics to rethink climate governance
records.abstract: Abstract This article explores the logics mobilized by stakeholders involved in national climate governance to identify ways of conciliating them for sound governance. Based on the theoretical framework of institutional logics, the study offers an innovative perspective on climate governance and the management of green funds. Content analysis of the briefs submitted ( N = 46) to a public hearing in Quebec (Canada) reveals three competing institutional logics: scientific governance, authority‐based governance, and participative governance. The results of this research have significant managerial and political implications for our understanding of the interactions between the different logics and for identifying ways to optimize climate governance. It also addresses essential but under‐researched aspects of national climate governance and green fund management.

records.abstract: As universities and governments seek to prepare the next generation of diplomats to manage international affairs, they finally have a teaching tool focusing on the practical knowledge and skills that in the past could be learned only on the job. records.title: (Mis)Understandings of defence diplomacy as public diplomacy: Insights from three Spanish elites
records.abstract: Defence diplomacy and public diplomacy are two diplomatic practices often treated in the literature as two disconnected realms. While the former focuses on the peaceful and cooperative use of armed forces, the latter emphasizes on the advancement of strategic communication in the international policy of actors. However, it is possible to bridge the differences between the two using the concept of soft power. By doing so, defence public diplomacy can be understood as a set of practices developed by states seeking to influence and attract third states while employing military force within these parameters. This paper contributes firstly to the conceptual debate bridging both types of diplomacies. Secondly, it selects a case study, Spain, to examine the perceptions of three different Spanish elites involved in the formulation and implementation of defence public policy: politicians, the military and defence industry managers. This paper adopts a qualitative methodology, including in-depth interviews, focus groups with experts, and manual content analysis of primary documentary sources. The results show that these elites agree on the importance of defence diplomacy for the achievement of state goals but continue to understand it fundamentally from a classical diplomatic prism. They also discuss the inclusion of new concepts, such as deterrence, as part of a defence public diplomacy.

records.abstract: Abstract This chapter focuses on the formal aspects of diplomatic relations. It details the precedence among heads of State and States, which considers the assumption that the papacy's precedence above other potentates next to the Emperor. Nowadays, no formal precedence is recognized among nations, so precedence among heads of diplomatic missions is determined by the date of their taking up their functions. Meanwhile, the United Nations have orders of precedence between delegates and officials and between member countries. The chapter discusses the selections of heads of mission and the utilization of Full Power, which is a special authorization from the head of the State they represent.
